newsitem.title: ITALY: TENNIS-ITALY STUN SPAIN WITH 2-0 LEAD IN DAVIS TIE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-ITALY STUN SPAIN WITH 2-0 LEAD IN DAVIS TIE.

text.p: Renzo Furlan left Spain in danger of a shock exit from the Davis Cup on Friday after beating Alberto Costa to give unfancied Italy a 2-0 lead in their world group quarter-final.
Compatriot Omar Camporese had earlier recovered from losing two tie-breaks to beat world number eight Carlos Moya and put the self-professed underdogs Italy ahead 1-0 in the opening singles match.

Furlan, ranked 64th, then finished off an astonishing night for Italy, beating 12th-ranked Costa 4-6 6-3 4-6 6-4 6-1 in another five-setter to give Italy a chance to wrap up the contest in Saturday's doubles.
Costa took a commanding 2-1 lead over Furlan, who saved three of four set points in the third set before finally hitting an unforced error into the net.
The fourth set went with serve until Costa, at 5-4 down, hit a forehand volley wide followed by two double faults to hand Furlan the set.
Furlan then piled on the pressure by breaking his opponent at the beginning of the final set. He wrapped up the win after three hours and seven minutes.
Veteran Camporese took longer, three hours and 42 minutes to be exact, and lost two tie-breaks to world number eight Carlos Moya before winning 6-7 (8-10) 6-7 (4-7) 6-1 6-3 6-3.
Camporese, 29, showed pressure in the first set tie-break against Moya and wasted two set points, the first on a lame double fault.

The 6,000 strong Italian crowd in the indoor arena vented their frustration at the umpire and cried out "shame" after an angry Camporese contested a series of close baseline calls in the highly-charged first tie-break.
Moya said he thought he would win handily after the second tie-break when the crowd fell silent.
"I won the first two sets easily...but after the fourth I began to think I'd lose. Things happen that way in the Davis Cup," the Spaniard said.
Moya, beaten finalist at this year's Australian Open, never showed the tennis he is capable of and relied instead on unforced errors from the Italian to build his lead.
At the start of the third set Camporese gestured to the crowd for more support and won it 6-1, scoring the first service break by either player after two hours and three minutes.
His confidence high, Camporese then repeatedly hit the baseline with his drives as he raced through the final two sets against a lacklustre Moya.
"I had nothing to lose," a tearful Camporese said.
"In front of me I had the world number eight. He had things to worry about."
Moya denied he had taken the game too easily after comments in the Italian press that Italy had no chance of victory.
"You have to take the Davis Cup seriously. Only the Italian press said Spain had an 80 percent chance of victory," he said.
